text: Most data work doesn't happen in a script you run top to bottom. It happens as a conversation: load some data, look at it, try a transformation, look again, draw a chart, adjust. A Jupyter notebook is built for exactly that rhythm — write a few lines of Python, run them, see the result directly underneath, then carry on from where you left off. This lesson covers how notebooks work, and the one trap that catches almost every beginner: hidden state.

Activate your project environment from Lesson 1, then install and launch JupyterLab with pip install jupyterlab, followed by jupyter lab. Your browser opens a workspace showing your project folder. Choose Python 3 under Notebook to create a new file with the dot i-p-y-n-b extension. The classic Jupyter Notebook interface, and the notebook editor built into VS Code, work the same way — everything here applies to all of them.

A notebook is a list of cells. Code cells hold Python — press Shift-Enter to run one and move to the next. Markdown cells hold formatted text: headings, bullet lists, explanations of why you're doing each step. Behind the notebook sits a kernel, a running Python process. Every code cell you run is sent to that one kernel, which remembers everything: every variable, every import, every function you've defined. That memory is what makes notebooks feel interactive — and it's also where the trouble starts.

When a cell finishes, Jupyter displays the value of the last expression automatically — you don't need print. Set total to 100 and write total times 2 on the next line, and the output shown underneath is 200. If you do use print, the printed text appears first, then the last expression's value after it. When the last expression is a pandas DataFrame, which you'll meet in Chapter 3, Jupyter renders it as a formatted table. Matplotlib charts show up inline too.

Because the kernel remembers everything, the order you run cells in matters, not the order they appear on the page. Set x to 10 in one cell, then in a second cell set x equal to x times 2 and display x. Run the first cell, then the second, and you see 20. Now run that second cell again without touching the first — you see 40, because x was already 20 when it ran a second time. Nothing on screen warns you the notebook has drifted from its top-to-bottom story.

Two habits prevent that drift. First, regularly choose Restart Kernel and Run All Cells from the Kernel menu — this wipes the memory and runs every cell from the top; if the notebook survives, it's trustworthy. Second, watch the number in brackets beside each code cell — it's the order the cells actually ran in, and jumbled numbers mean a jumbled story. IPython's magic commands help too: percent-timeit times a statement, and a line starting with an exclamation mark runs in the system shell.

A notebook file is JSON that stores your code and, by default, the outputs from its last run — convenient for sharing, inconvenient for version control, which we handle in Chapter 7. Remember: a notebook saved with outputs still needs a clean Restart and Run All before you trust it. Next lesson: variables, types, and control flow — the core of the Python language itself.
